questions.title: The ball that bounces higher than it was dropped
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.2 Forces and momentum (Newton's laws, momentum, impulse, conservation of momentum in elastic collisions)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: The light ball rebounds to about eight times its drop height rather than to the drop height, because the elastic floor bounce sends the heavy ball upwards while the light one is still falling, so their relative approach speed is $2v$ and the second elastic collision reverses it; the exact rebound factor $(3M-m)/(M+m)$ is not set by the drop height and has to be derived rather than guessed.

questions.question: A small ball of mass $m=0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests lightly on top of a large ball of mass $M=1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. The two balls are released from rest together and both fall through a height $h=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ before the large ball reaches a hard horizontal floor; the balls are small compared with $h$, so they stay on the same vertical line throughout. The large ball strikes the floor and rebounds; that collision is perfectly elastic, so the large ball leaves the floor moving upwards with the same speed it had just before impact. At that instant the small ball has not yet reached the floor and is still moving downwards. The two balls then collide along the vertical line, and that collision is also perfectly elastic. Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that, just before the two balls collide, the large ball is moving upwards at speed $v$ and the small ball is moving downwards at the same speed $v$, where $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, and calculate the value of $v$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By conserving momentum and using the fact that, for a perfectly elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, show that the velocity of the small ball immediately after the collision is $w=\dfrac{(3M-m)v}{M+m}$ upwards, and calculate the value of $w$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the maximum height above the floor reached by the small ball, express it as a multiple of $h$, and explain why it is greater than $h$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the multiple of $h$ found in part (c) tends to $9$ as $M/m\to\infty$, and state the largest multiple of $h$ that any mass ratio can give.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The large ball falls freely through a height $h$, so just before it reaches the floor its speed is $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. **(M1)**

The floor collision is perfectly elastic, so the large ball leaves the floor with speed $v$ directed upwards. The small ball has fallen through the same height and is still in free fall, so it is moving downwards at the same speed $v$. **(A1)**

$$v=\sqrt{2\times 9.81\times 0.20}=\sqrt{3.924}=1.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Take upwards as positive. Immediately before the collision between the balls the large ball has velocity $+v$ and the small ball has velocity $-v$; let their velocities immediately afterwards be $V$ and $w$. **(M1)**

Conservation of momentum:

$$Mv+m(-v)=MV+mw\quad\Rightarrow\quad MV+mw=(M-m)v$$ **(M1)**

For a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach:

$$w-V=v-(-v)=2v\quad\Rightarrow\quad V=w-2v$$ **(M1)**

Substituting this into the momentum equation:

$$M(w-2v)+mw=(M-m)v\quad\Rightarrow\quad (M+m)w=(3M-m)v$$

$$w=\frac{(3M-m)v}{M+m}$$ **(AG)**

Numerically,

$$w=\frac{3.0-0.050}{1.050}(1.981)=\frac{2.95}{1.050}(1.981)=2.810(1.981)=5.57\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

directed upwards. (The large ball recoils upwards at $V=\dfrac{M-3m}{M+m}v=\dfrac{0.85}{1.05}(1.981)=1.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.)

**(c)** The small ball leaves the collision with speed $w$ upwards, so it rises to

$$H=\frac{w^{2}}{2g}=\frac{(5.565)^{2}}{2\times 9.81}=\frac{30.97}{19.62}=1.58\ \mathrm{m}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

As a multiple of the drop height, $H/h=1.58/0.20=7.89$. **(A1)**

This is far greater than $h$ because the small ball gains energy from the large ball. In the large ball's frame the small ball approaches with relative speed $2v$, and the elastic collision reverses that relative velocity, so the small ball leaves at close to $v+2v=3v$ when $M\gg m$. Its kinetic energy is therefore much larger than the $\frac12 mv^{2}$ it had on landing, and the extra energy is drawn from the much larger kinetic energy of the large ball. **(A1)**

**(d)** Dividing numerator and denominator by $M$,

$$\frac{3M-m}{M+m}=\frac{3-m/M}{1+m/M}\to 3\quad\text{as }M/m\to\infty,$$ **(M1)**

so $w\to 3v$ and $H\to \dfrac{(3v)^{2}}{2g}=9\dfrac{v^{2}}{2g}=9h$. **(A1)** The largest multiple of $h$ that any mass ratio can give is therefore $9$. **(A1)** For a finite ratio the multiple is smaller: here $M/m=20$ gives only $7.89$, and a real stacked-ball drop gives far less still because neither collision is perfectly elastic and air resistance removes energy.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ from free fall. The (A1) requires both statements: the floor bounce is elastic, so the large ball's speed is unchanged in magnitude and reversed in direction, and the small ball is still falling at $v$. A candidate who assumes the small ball has already reached the floor or has stopped has misread the geometry and earns nothing after the first mark. Accept $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) The (AG) requires both conservation laws to be used. A candidate who simply writes down the standard elastic result $w=(3M-m)v/(M+m)$ with no justification earns at most one (M1). Accept any consistent sign convention provided the final direction is stated. A candidate who treats the collision as perfectly inelastic and uses a common velocity afterwards obtains $w=(M-m)v/(M+m)=0.905v$ and forfeits the last three marks. Follow-through applies: if the algebra is sound but the arithmetic slips, credit the numerical (A1).

(c) Follow-through from (b) is allowed. The final (A1) requires a physical reason referring either to energy transferred from the large ball or to the reversal of the relative velocity; 'because it bounces off two balls' is not sufficient.

(d) The limit must be shown, not quoted: award (M1) for dividing numerator and denominator by $M$. Accept $9h$ or $9$. Do not accept 'infinity' or 'it keeps increasing' — the ratio is bounded.
questions.explanation:
The result is genuinely surprising: a ball dropped from $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ rises to $1.58\ \mathrm{m}$, nearly eight times its drop height, with no energy input. Students who have met a bouncing-ball problem usually expect the small ball to return to roughly $h$, or at most to $4h$ if they mis-apply a factor of two. The point is that there are two collisions, not one, and the second one is elastic.

The key insight is to work in the large ball's frame. After the floor bounce the large ball moves upwards at $v$ while the small ball is still moving downwards at $v$, so the relative approach speed is $2v$. In a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach, so the small ball leaves with relative speed $2v$. Because the large ball is heavy its own velocity barely changes, so in the ground frame the small ball leaves at about $v+2v=3v$. Squaring gives nine times the kinetic energy, hence $9h$.

The exact calculation replaces 'about' with the mass-ratio factor $(3M-m)/(M+m)$. With $M/m=20$ this factor is $2.81$ rather than $3$, so the height is $7.89h$ rather than $9h$; the ideal figure is only approached as the large ball becomes infinitely heavy. A candidate who quotes $9h$ without doing the mass-ratio arithmetic has answered the limiting question, not the one asked, and the markscheme separates the exact value from the limit deliberately.

The classic wrong turns are: assuming the small ball has already landed when the large ball bounces; applying momentum conservation but not the relative-velocity condition, which leaves one equation for two unknowns; and treating the second collision as perfectly inelastic. There is also a real-world check worth making: an actual stacked-ball drop gives far less than $7.9h$ because the coefficient of restitution is well below one and air resistance matters, so the idealised model is an upper bound rather than a prediction.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the A.2 bullets on conservation of momentum and elastic collisions. The design was constructed backwards from the exact rebound factor $(3M-m)/(M+m)$: the masses $M=1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $m=0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$ were chosen so that the mass ratio $M/m=20$ makes the exact factor $2.81$ visibly different from the limiting value $3$, and $h=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ makes the rebound height a checkable $1.58\ \mathrm{m}$. The two-stage geometry, the relative-velocity route and the limit part are original.

verification.method: Both collisions solved from momentum plus relative-velocity reversal; the post-collision velocities were re-checked against conservation of momentum and of kinetic energy, and the rebound height recomputed from H = w^2/(2g).

questions.title: Why the conveyor motor needs twice the power you expect
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.3 Work, energy and power (work done by a force, conservation of energy, power as the rate of energy transfer, efficiency)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: The motor power is not the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy but twice that, because the belt's friction force acts through the belt's displacement while the gravel slides and lags behind, so exactly half of the energy supplied is dissipated as heat at the sliding surface and the efficiency is pinned at 50 per cent.
questions.stimulus: Gravel falls vertically from a stationary hopper onto a horizontal conveyor belt that runs at a constant speed. The gravel arrives with no horizontal velocity and is carried away at the belt's speed. In the steady state the mass of gravel delivered to the belt is $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ each second. Treat the gravel as arriving with no horizontal motion, neglect the mass and any internal friction of the belt mechanism, and consider the horizontal motion only.

questions.question: The belt moves at a constant speed $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the gravel is delivered at a constant rate of $12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the horizontal force the belt must exert on the gravel is $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, and calculate the value of $F$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied to the gravel as it is brought up to the belt's speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the power delivered by the belt's motor is twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy, identify where the remaining energy goes, and hence calculate the efficiency with which the motor's work becomes kinetic energy of the gravel.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The belt speed is increased to $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while the mass flow rate is unchanged. Determine the new motor power and explain why it is not simply double the original power.

questions.answer:
**(a)** In a time interval $\Delta t$ a mass $\Delta m=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\Delta t$ of gravel is brought from rest to the belt's speed $v$. Its horizontal momentum therefore changes by $\Delta m\,v$, so the required horizontal force is

$$F=\frac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t}=v\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$$ **(M1)(AG)**

Numerically,

$$F=2.0\times 12=24\ \mathrm{N}$$ **(A1)(A1)**

**(b)** Each second a mass of $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest to $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied is

$$\frac{\Delta E_{k}}{\Delta t}=\tfrac12\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}=\tfrac12(12)(2.0)^{2}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

$$=24\ \mathrm{W}$$ **(A1)(A1)**

**(c)** The belt moves at constant speed, so the motor's power equals the force it exerts multiplied by the belt's speed:

$$P=Fv=(24)(2.0)=48\ \mathrm{W}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

The ratio is

$$\frac{P}{\Delta E_{k}/\Delta t}=\frac{48}{24}=2$$ **(A1)**

so the motor supplies twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy. The remaining $24\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated as heat where the gravel slides against the belt while it is being accelerated: the friction force acts over the belt's displacement, which is larger than the gravel's displacement, and the difference appears as thermal energy at the sliding contact. **(A1)** The efficiency is therefore

$$\eta=\frac{24}{48}=0.50=50\%.$$ **(A1)**

**(d)** Since $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, doubling $v$ doubles the force to $48\ \mathrm{N}$. The power is $P=Fv$, and both the force and the belt speed have doubled, so

$$P=48\times 4.0=192\ \mathrm{W},$$ **(M1)(A1)**

which is four times the original $48\ \mathrm{W}$. Equivalently $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}\propto v^{2}$, because the belt must accelerate twice as much momentum each second and must do so through twice the distance per second. The mass flow rate has not changed, so the factor of four comes entirely from the doubling of both quantities in $P=Fv$, not from any change in the amount of gravel handled. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The force must come from the rate of change of momentum, not from an energy argument. A candidate who writes $F=\tfrac12\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v=12\ \mathrm{N}$ has used the kinetic-energy rate and has made the very error the question is designed to expose; award no method mark. Accept $F=v\Delta m/\Delta t$ with $\Delta m/\Delta t=12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) Accept $24\ \mathrm{W}$, $24\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ or $24\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-1}}$. A candidate who uses $mv^{2}$ instead of $\tfrac12 mv^{2}$ obtains $48\ \mathrm{W}$ and will then report a 100% efficiency; that contradiction should prompt a re-check but earns nothing here.

(c) The essential reasoning is that the belt's force acts through the belt's displacement, not the gravel's. Simply stating 'half the energy is lost as heat' without identifying the sliding contact earns at most one mark. Award the efficiency mark for $0.50$ or $50\%$; a ratio written the other way round ($2$) with a clear statement is acceptable. Follow-through: if (a) or (b) is wrong but internally consistent, the ratio and efficiency marks remain available.

(d) The explanation must mention both that $F\propto v$ and that the belt speed is $v$, so that $P\propto v^{2}$. A candidate who says only 'because power depends on $v$ squared' earns the value mark but not the explanation mark. Accept $192\ \mathrm{W}$ and accept $190\ \mathrm{W}$.
questions.explanation:
This question is built on a result that contradicts the energy audit most students perform automatically. The gravel gains kinetic energy at $24\ \mathrm{W}$, so it is natural to conclude that the motor must supply $24\ \mathrm{W}$. It does not: the motor supplies $48\ \mathrm{W}$, and the other $24\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated as heat where the gravel slides against the belt.

The reason is that work is force multiplied by the displacement of the point of application. The belt's friction force acts on the gravel, but the belt itself moves further than the gravel does while the gravel is catching up. In one second the belt advances $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$, whereas the gravel being accelerated moves on average only $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$, so the motor does $24\ \mathrm{N}\times 2.0\ \mathrm{m}=48\ \mathrm{J}$ of work while the gravel's kinetic energy rises by only $24\ \mathrm{J}$. The difference is the frictional heating at the sliding interface.

This is the same mechanism that heats a car's clutch during a standing start, and it is why the efficiency of any device that picks up a fresh charge of mass from rest by dragging it along at a fixed speed is capped at 50%. It is not a machine fault; it is a consequence of the inelastic way the mass is acquired.

Part (d) turns the result into a scaling law. The force is $F=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v$, proportional to $v$, and the power is $Fv$, so $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}$. Doubling the belt speed therefore doubles the force and doubles the speed through which that force acts, giving four times the power — a trap for candidates who expect a linear response.

Classic wrong turns: using $\tfrac12 mv^{2}$ to find the force; forgetting that it is the belt's displacement, not the gravel's, that sets the work done by the motor; and assuming that a constant-speed belt does no net work because the gravel's kinetic energy ends up steady. That last error confuses a steady state with a closed system.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the A.3 bullets on work, power and efficiency, combined with the A.2 idea of force as the rate of change of momentum. The design is original in its arc: the force is obtained from momentum, the kinetic-energy rate is then contrasted with the motor power to expose the factor of two, the missing energy is located at the sliding contact, and the final part converts the result into the scaling law $P\propto v^{2}$. The values $12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ and $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ were chosen so that the force, the kinetic-energy rate and the motor power come out as $24\ \mathrm{N}$, $24\ \mathrm{W}$ and $48\ \mathrm{W}$ exactly.

verification.method: Force, kinetic-energy rate and motor power recomputed from F = v dm/dt, dEk/dt = 0.5 (dm/dt) v^2 and P = Fv; the energy balance 48 W = 24 W (kinetic) + 24 W (heat) was checked, and the v^2 scaling re-derived at 4.0 m/s.

questions.title: Two readings in a vacuum chamber: emissivity and specific heat
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.1 Thermal energy transfers (specific heat capacity, latent heat, conduction, convection, radiation, Stefan-Boltzmann law)
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The cooling rate is not set by the temperature difference the student reaches for but by the difference of the fourth powers, and the specific heat capacity is recovered from the instantaneous energy balance at the very temperature at which the emissivity was fixed, so the two unknowns separate only once the student realises the radiated power is the same in both experiments.
questions.stimulus:
A block of an unknown alloy is suspended by a fine thread inside a chamber that has been evacuated and whose walls are held at a constant temperature. An electric heater inside the block supplies a constant power. The following values are measured.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| mass of the block, $m$ | $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ |
| total surface area, $A$ | $0.020\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$ |
| electrical power supplied, $P$ | $15.0\ \mathrm{W}$ |
| wall temperature, $T_{\text{wall}}$ | $300\ \mathrm{K}$ |
| steady temperature of the block, $T_{s}$ | $420\ \mathrm{K}$ |
| initial rate of fall of temperature at $420\ \mathrm{K}$, after the heater is switched off | $0.130\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$ |
| Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\sigma$ | $5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$ |

figure.caption: The block is suspended by a fine thread inside an evacuated chamber. The walls are held at 300 K and the block loses energy by radiation only.
figure.content: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="A heated block suspended inside an evacuated chamber whose walls are held at 300 K"><rect x="70" y="40" width="320" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="80" y="32" font-size="11" fill="#1e293b">evacuated chamber</text><text x="230" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">walls at 300 K</text><line x1="230" y1="40" x2="230" y2="86" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><rect x="190" y="120" width="80" height="70" rx="6" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="230" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#0f172a">block</text><text x="230" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a">0.50 kg</text><text x="230" y="181" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a">A = 0.020 m2</text><line x1="190" y1="155" x2="150" y2="155" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="128" y="152" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">heater</text><text x="128" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">15.0 W</text><g stroke="#0f766e" stroke-width="1.1"><line x1="200" y1="120" x2="200" y2="90"/><line x1="230" y1="120" x2="230" y2="90"/><line x1="260" y1="120" x2="260" y2="90"/></g><text x="330" y="105" font-size="10" fill="#0f766e">radiated power</text><line x1="230" y1="228" x2="230" y2="208" stroke="#0f766e" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="230" y="262" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#475569">fine insulating thread (conduction neglected)</text></svg>

questions.question: The chamber is evacuated so that the block loses energy to the walls by radiation only, and conduction along the supporting thread is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, with the chamber evacuated, conduction and convection can be neglected and the block loses energy only by radiation, and state the expression for the net power radiated by the block.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The block reaches a steady temperature of $420\ \mathrm{K}$. Show that the emissivity of its surface is $\varepsilon=0.575$, and calculate the value of $\varepsilon$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heater is switched off when the block is at $420\ \mathrm{K}$ and the temperature then falls at an initial rate of $0.130\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$. Determine the specific heat capacity of the alloy, explaining why the radiated power at this instant is the same as during the steady state.

parts.label: d
parts.text: When the block has cooled to $360\ \mathrm{K}$, determine the rate of fall of temperature predicted by the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the ratio of this rate to the rate at $420\ \mathrm{K}$. Explain why a model in which the rate is proportional to $(T-T_{\text{wall}})$ predicts a different ratio.

questions.answer:
**(a)** In an evacuated chamber there is no gas to conduct heat or to carry it by convection, and radiation is the only transfer mechanism that needs no medium. **(A1)** The block emits $\varepsilon\sigma A T^{4}$ and absorbs $\varepsilon\sigma A T_{\text{wall}}^{4}$ from the walls, **(A1)** so the net power it loses is

$$P_{\text{rad}}=\varepsilon\sigma A\left(T^{4}-T_{\text{wall}}^{4}\right).$$ **(A1)**

**(b)** At steady state the electrical power supplied is exactly balanced by the net radiated power:

$$P=\varepsilon\sigma A\left(T_{s}^{4}-T_{\text{wall}}^{4}\right)$$ **(M1)**

$$\varepsilon=\frac{P}{\sigma A\left(T_{s}^{4}-T_{\text{wall}}^{4}\right)}$$ **(A1)**

$$\varepsilon=\frac{15.0}{5.67\times10^{-8}\times 0.020\times\left(3.1117\times10^{10}-8.100\times10^{9}\right)}$$ **(A1)**

$$=\frac{15.0}{5.67\times10^{-8}\times 0.020\times 2.3017\times10^{10}}=\frac{15.0}{26.10}=0.575$$ **(A1)**

**(c)** At the instant the heater is switched off the block is still at $420\ \mathrm{K}$, and the net radiated power depends only on the temperatures of the block and the walls, so it is unchanged at $15.0\ \mathrm{W}$. **(M1)** The thermal energy of the block now falls at a rate $mc\left|\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}\right|$, and this must equal the radiated power:

$$mc\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}=\varepsilon\sigma A\left(T_{s}^{4}-T_{\text{wall}}^{4}\right)=15.0\ \mathrm{W}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

$$c=\frac{15.0}{m\,\Delta T/\Delta t}=\frac{15.0}{0.50\times 0.130}=\frac{15.0}{0.065}$$ **(A1)**

$$=231\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

**(d)** At $360\ \mathrm{K}$,

$$P=\varepsilon\sigma A\left(360^{4}-300^{4}\right)=0.5747\times 5.67\times10^{-8}\times 0.020\times\left(1.6796\times10^{10}-8.100\times10^{9}\right)$$ **(M1)**

$$=0.5747\times 5.67\times10^{-8}\times 0.020\times 8.6962\times10^{9}=5.67\ \mathrm{W}$$ **(A1)**

$$\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}=\frac{P}{mc}=\frac{5.67}{0.50\times 230.8}=0.0491\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

so the ratio to the rate at $420\ \mathrm{K}$ is $\dfrac{0.0491}{0.130}=0.378$. A model in which the rate is proportional to $\left(T-T_{\text{wall}}\right)$ would instead give $\dfrac{360-300}{420-300}=\dfrac{60}{120}=0.50$. **(A1)** The two predictions differ by about 30%, and it is the $T^{4}$ prediction that fits the data, because the radiated power falls with the difference of the fourth powers of the absolute temperatures rather than with their difference.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The three (A1)s are for: radiation needs no medium, so an evacuated chamber removes conduction and convection; the surface emits $\varepsilon\sigma A T^{4}$; and the net loss subtracts the absorbed $\varepsilon\sigma A T_{\text{wall}}^{4}$. A candidate who omits the wall term and uses $P=\varepsilon\sigma A T^{4}$ alone has forgotten that the walls also radiate onto the block; this is a common and significant error and it forfeits the third mark.

(b) The (AG) requires the steady-state condition 'electrical power in equals net radiative power out' to be stated. Award the emissivity marks for $\varepsilon$ between $0.570$ and $0.580$. Do not accept a value obtained with the wrong surface area.

(c) The crucial step is recognising that the radiated power at $420\ \mathrm{K}$ is the same $15.0\ \mathrm{W}$ whether the heater is on or off, because it depends only on the block and wall temperatures. A candidate who tries to subtract something from $15.0\ \mathrm{W}$ forfeits the method mark. Accept $c$ in the range $225$–$237\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Follow-through applies from (b): if the candidate's $\varepsilon$ differs, their $c$ will be consistent with it and should be credited.

(d) Accept $0.047$–$0.051\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$ for the rate and $0.37$–$0.39$ for the ratio. The final comparison mark requires both numbers to be stated; 'the $T^{4}$ law fits better' without the linear prediction of $0.50$ earns only one mark. Do not penalise a candidate who compares the rates themselves rather than the ratios, provided the comparison is quantitative. A candidate who uses temperatures in degrees Celsius in the fourth-power term loses the two value marks.
questions.explanation:
The question uses a single apparatus to yield two material properties, and the reason it works is worth stating clearly: the radiated power depends only on the temperatures of the block and the walls, so at the moment the heater is switched off — when the block is still at $420\ \mathrm{K}$ — the radiated power is exactly the $15.0\ \mathrm{W}$ the heater was supplying. Nothing about the heating itself has to be modelled; the energy balance does the work.

The first trap is the term that is missing. Students who have met the black-body formula reach for $P=\varepsilon\sigma A T^{4}$ and forget that the walls radiate back. The net loss is $\varepsilon\sigma A\left(T^{4}-T_{\text{wall}}^{4}\right)$. At $420\ \mathrm{K}$ with walls at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ the wall term is 26% of the surface term, so ignoring it changes the emissivity by a quarter — this is not a rounding error.

The second trap is assuming that the cooling rate is proportional to the temperature difference. That is the linear 'Newton's law of cooling' intuition, and it is wrong for radiation. At $360\ \mathrm{K}$ the temperature difference above the walls is half what it was at $420\ \mathrm{K}$, so the linear model predicts the cooling rate to halve. The $T^{4}$ law predicts a ratio of $0.378$, and the difference is easily measurable. The reason is that the radiated power depends on the fourth power of the absolute temperature, so as the block cools the emitted power collapses much faster than the temperature difference does.

The third point is that the two unknowns decouple only because both measurements are made at $420\ \mathrm{K}$. Had the cooling rate been measured at some other temperature, the student would have to carry the $T^{4}$ ratio through the algebra; measuring at the same temperature makes the radiative term cancel, which is exactly the kind of experimental-design decision the question is testing.

Classic wrong turns: using $P=\varepsilon\sigma A T^{4}$ without the wall term; inserting temperatures in degrees Celsius into the fourth-power term; and assuming the cooling curve is exponential when in fact it is not.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the B.1 bullets on specific heat capacity, radiation and the Stefan-Boltzmann law. The two-reading design is the original element: the same steady temperature supplies the emissivity through the radiative balance and the specific heat capacity through the instantaneous cooling rate, which only works because both are measured at $420\ \mathrm{K}$. The values were chosen so that the emissivity is $0.575$, the specific heat capacity is $231\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and the $T^{4}$ cooling ratio is $0.378$ against a linear-model prediction of $0.50$.

verification.method: Emissivity from eps = P/(sigma A (Ts^4 - Tw^4)) = 15.0/26.10 = 0.5747; specific heat capacity from c = P/(m dT/dt) = 15.0/0.065 = 230.8 J/kg/K; the 360 K rate recomputed as eps*sigma*A*(360^4-300^4)/(mc) = 5.667/115.4 = 0.0491 K/s, ratio 0.378 against the linear prediction 0.50.

questions.title: The layer that adds a fixed factor to the surface temperature
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.2 Greenhouse effect (planetary energy balance, albedo, emissivity, surface temperature, one-layer atmosphere model)
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The greenhouse warming factor is not set by the albedo or the solar constant that students reach for, because the surface temperature is always exactly $2^{1/4}$ times the effective radiating temperature, so changing the albedo moves both temperatures together while leaving their ratio untouched.
questions.stimulus: A spherical planet of radius $R$ orbits its star. At the planet's distance the solar constant is $S=1.36\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and the planetary albedo is $\alpha=0.30$. The planet rotates rapidly, so its surface and its atmosphere may each be treated as having a single uniform temperature. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$.

questions.question: The planet has no internal heat source, and in the steady state the power it absorbs from its star equals the power it radiates to space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By balancing the solar power intercepted by the planet against the power it radiates to space, show that the effective radiating temperature $T_{e}$ satisfies $T_{e}^{4}=\dfrac{S(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}$, and calculate the value of $T_{e}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The planet has a single layer of atmosphere that is transparent to sunlight but absorbs all the infrared radiation emitted by the surface, radiating equally upwards and downwards. By considering the energy balance of the layer and of the surface, show that the surface temperature is $T_{s}=2^{1/4}T_{e}$, and calculate the value of $T_{s}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the surface temperature if the albedo were $0.34$ instead of $0.30$, and determine the ratio $T_{s}/T_{e}$ in each case.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The one-layer model predicts a surface temperature that is higher than the observed mean surface temperature of the real planet. Evaluate the model, suggesting one reason why it overestimates the warming and one feature of a real atmosphere that a single layer cannot represent.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Sunlight is intercepted over the planet's cross-sectional area $\pi R^{2}$, so the power absorbed is $P_{\text{abs}}=S\pi R^{2}(1-\alpha)$. **(M1)** The planet radiates from its whole surface, of area $4\pi R^{2}$, at the effective temperature $T_{e}$, so $P_{\text{emit}}=4\pi R^{2}\sigma T_{e}^{4}$. **(M1)** In equilibrium $P_{\text{abs}}=P_{\text{emit}}$:

$$S\pi R^{2}(1-\alpha)=4\pi R^{2}\sigma T_{e}^{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{e}^{4}=\frac{S(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}$$ **(M1)(AG)**

$$T_{e}^{4}=\frac{1.36\times10^{3}\times 0.70}{4\times 5.67\times10^{-8}}=\frac{952}{2.268\times10^{-7}}=4.20\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{K^{4}}$$

$$T_{e}=255\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Let $T_{a}$ be the temperature of the layer. The layer absorbs $\sigma T_{s}^{4}$ per unit area from the surface and radiates $\sigma T_{a}^{4}$ upwards and $\sigma T_{a}^{4}$ downwards, so **(M1)**

$$\sigma T_{s}^{4}=2\sigma T_{a}^{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{a}^{4}=\frac{T_{s}^{4}}{2}$$ **(A1)**

At the top of the atmosphere the only power leaving is the upward radiation of the layer, which must equal the absorbed solar power per unit area: **(M1)**

$$\sigma T_{a}^{4}=\frac{S(1-\alpha)}{4}=\sigma T_{e}^{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{a}=T_{e}$$

At the surface, the power absorbed is the sunlight $\dfrac{S(1-\alpha)}{4}$ plus the downward radiation from the layer, $\sigma T_{a}^{4}=\sigma T_{e}^{4}$: **(M1)**

$$\sigma T_{s}^{4}=\sigma T_{e}^{4}+\sigma T_{e}^{4}=2\sigma T_{e}^{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{s}=2^{1/4}T_{e}$$ **(AG)**

$$T_{s}=1.189\times 255=303\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(A1)**

**(c)** With $\alpha=0.34$,

$$T_{e}^{4}=\frac{1.36\times10^{3}\times 0.66}{4\times 5.67\times10^{-8}}=3.96\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{K^{4}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{e}=251\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(M1)**

$$T_{s}=2^{1/4}\times 251=298\ \mathrm{K}$$ **(A1)**

The ratio is $T_{s}/T_{e}=2^{1/4}=1.19$ in both cases. **(A1)** It is unchanged because the factor $2^{1/4}$ arises from the geometry of the layer, not from the amount of sunlight reaching the planet.

**(d)** The model gives $303\ \mathrm{K}$ against an observed mean surface temperature of $288\ \mathrm{K}$, so it overestimates the warming above the effective temperature by about $15\ \mathrm{K}$. **(A1)** A single layer that absorbs all the infrared and is isothermal is an extremely strong absorber: it intercepts every photon leaving the surface and sends half of them back down, which maximises the back-radiation. A real atmosphere absorbs only in certain wavelength bands, so much of the surface radiation escapes directly to space through the atmospheric window, and the effective number of absorbing layers is far smaller than one fully opaque layer. **(A1)** In addition, a real atmosphere has a temperature that falls with height and is cooled by convection, which carries energy upwards and shortens the path over which the greenhouse effect operates — a feature that a single isothermal layer cannot represent. **(A1)** The model is nevertheless useful: it reproduces the correct order of magnitude and, more importantly, the correct qualitative result that the surface is warmer than the effective radiating temperature. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The three (M1)/(AG) marks are for the intercepted area $\pi R^{2}$, the emitting area $4\pi R^{2}$ and the equilibrium condition. A candidate who omits the factor of four obtains $T_{e}=360\ \mathrm{K}$; this is the single most common error and it loses the final two marks. The (AG) requires the two areas to be shown explicitly, not merely asserted. Accept $T_{e}=254$–$256\ \mathrm{K}$ and accept $255\ \mathrm{K}$.

(b) The layer's balance must be written as 'absorbs $\sigma T_{s}^{4}$, radiates $2\sigma T_{a}^{4}$'. A candidate who writes the layer balance as $\sigma T_{s}^{4}=\sigma T_{a}^{4}$, radiating upwards only, obtains $T_{s}=T_{e}$ and loses the method marks; the doubling is the entire content of the greenhouse effect. The surface balance must include the absorbed sunlight as well as the back-radiation. Follow-through applies from (a): a candidate whose $T_{e}$ is wrong but whose factor $2^{1/4}$ is correct earns the (AG) and the final (A1) on their own value.

(c) Accept $T_{e}=250$–$252\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{s}=297$–$299\ \mathrm{K}$. The key mark is the observation that the ratio is unchanged; a candidate who reports a different ratio has made an arithmetic slip. Do not accept a ratio quoted as $1.19$ with no justification for its constancy.

(d) The evaluation must name a specific deficiency, not merely say 'it is only a model'. Credit any of: partial absorption and the atmospheric window; convection and the lapse rate; clouds; the layer not being isothermal; multiple absorbing layers. Accept the numerical comparison of $303\ \mathrm{K}$ with $288\ \mathrm{K}$. Do not credit 'the model is wrong' without a mechanism.
questions.explanation:
The two-step structure of this question mirrors the physics of the greenhouse effect, and the pay-off is in part (c). The planet intercepts sunlight over a disc of area $\pi R^{2}$ but radiates from a sphere of area $4\pi R^{2}$. That mismatch of areas is the whole reason the effective radiating temperature is not the value you would get from $S(1-\alpha)/\sigma$; it is lower by a factor $4^{1/4}=1.41$. Students who omit the factor of four obtain $360\ \mathrm{K}$ and never notice, because $360\ \mathrm{K}$ is a plausible-looking planetary temperature.

The second step is the greenhouse layer. The layer absorbs all the infrared coming up from the surface and radiates it both ways, so half comes back down. Adding that back-radiation to the sunlight absorbed at the surface raises the surface temperature above the effective temperature, and the factor is exactly $2^{1/4}=1.19$. The derivation requires two separate energy balances — one for the layer, one for the surface — and candidates who try to shortcut by balancing only the top of the atmosphere never see the factor of two appear.

Part (c) is where the lever bites. Changing the albedo from $0.30$ to $0.34$ cools the planet, but it moves $T_{e}$ and $T_{s}$ together: the ratio $T_{s}/T_{e}$ is fixed at $2^{1/4}$ and is completely independent of the albedo and of the solar constant. This is genuinely counter-intuitive, because a student who expects a more reflective planet to have a weaker greenhouse effect will look for the ratio to change. It cannot: in the one-layer model the amplification depends only on the geometry of the layer, not on how much sunlight is available. The only way to change the factor is to change the model — more absorbing layers, partial absorption, or a non-isothermal atmosphere.

Part (d) then asks for judgement rather than calculation. The model predicts $303\ \mathrm{K}$ against an observed $288\ \mathrm{K}$, overestimating the warming by about $15\ \mathrm{K}$. The reasons are physical: real greenhouse gases absorb only in bands, so an atmospheric window lets surface radiation escape; the atmosphere is cooled by convection and has a lapse rate; and clouds and multiple layers complicate the picture. Recognising that a model can be quantitatively wrong and still capture the essential mechanism is the point of the part.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the B.2 bullets on planetary energy balance, albedo, emissivity and surface temperature. The arc is original: the effective temperature is derived with the $\pi R^{2}$ against $4\pi R^{2}$ area argument, the one-layer atmosphere is then derived from two separate energy balances, and the final parts exploit the fact that the greenhouse factor $2^{1/4}$ is independent of albedo. The values $S=1.36\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\alpha=0.30$ and $\alpha=0.34$ were chosen so that the effective temperature is a checkable $255\ \mathrm{K}$ and the surface temperature $303\ \mathrm{K}$, against the real planet's observed $288\ \mathrm{K}$.

verification.method: Effective temperature from Te = (S(1-a)/(4 sigma))^(1/4) = (4.1975e9)^(1/4) = 254.5 K; surface temperature Te * 2^(1/4) = 302.7 K; with a = 0.34, Te = 250.8 K and Ts = 298.3 K; the ratio Ts/Te = 2^(1/4) = 1.1892 in both cases.
